Blumenthal said the regulation would put women's health care at risk and would undercut state contraception laws. He said the regulation "intentionally shrouds" abortion in "new and unnecessary ambiguity," encouraging individuals to define it and to "deny virtually all forms of contraceptions, even emergency contraception to rape victims." The Planned Parenthood Federation of America and American Civil Liberties Union, which was acting on behalf of the National Family Planning & Reproductive Health Association, also filed separate suits Thursday. The Department of Health and Human Services said the regulation would allow the federal government to withhold federal funds for state and local governments, health plans and health care facilities that do not follow existing federal laws that ban discrimination against doctors and other health workers who refuse to participate in procedures such as sterilizations or abortions or to make referrals for such procedures. "We have not had an opportunity to review the lawsuits and we will respond to the court on any pending litigation," department spokeswoman Rebecca Ayers said in an e-mail. "The department followed appropriate procedures to put the regulation in place and the regulation is fully supported by law." The department promulgated the rule last month. "Doctors and other health care providers should not be forced to choose between good professional standing and violating their conscience," Health and Human Services Secretary Mike Leavitt said in a statement then. "This rule protects the right of medical providers to care for their patients in accord with their conscience." The department has said that it believes the public and health care providers are unaware of the federal anti-discrimination laws. "Many health care providers routinely face pressure to change their medical practice -- often in direct opposition to their personal convictions," said the department's assistant secretary of health, Adm. Joxel Garcia, in a statement in December. "During my practice as an OB-GYN, I witnessed this firsthand. Health care providers shouldn't have to check their consciences at the hospital door. Fortunately, Congress enacted several laws to that end, but too many are unaware these protections exist."

(CNN) — Seven states and two organizations have sued the Bush administration in an effort to block a federal regulation that would provide additional protections for health care workers who refuse, on religious or moral grounds, to perform abortions or other medical procedures.

The rule, which protects health care providers who decline to participate in certain procedures, has come under fire.

Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal filed a lawsuit Thursday on behalf of his state, as well as California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Oregon and Rhode Island. Blumenthal said the regulation would jeopardize women’s health care and undermine state contraception laws.

“On its way out, the Bush administration has left a ticking legal time bomb set to explode literally the day of the inaugural and blow apart vital constitutional rights and women’s health care,” Blumenthal said in a statement. “Women’s health may be endangered — needlessly and unlawfully — if this rule is allowed to stand.”

He said the regulation “intentionally shrouds” abortion in “new and unnecessary ambiguity,” encouraging individuals to define it themselves and to “deny virtually all forms of contraceptions, even emergency contraception to rape victims.”

The Planned Parenthood Federation of America and the American Civil Liberties Union, acting on behalf of the National Family Planning & Reproductive Health Association, also filed separate lawsuits Thursday.

The Department of Health and Human Services said the regulation would permit the federal government to withhold funding from state and local governments, health plans and health care facilities that fail to comply with existing federal laws prohibiting discrimination against doctors and other health care workers who refuse to participate in procedures such as sterilizations or abortions, or to provide referrals for such procedures.

“We have not had an opportunity to review the lawsuits and we will respond to the court on any pending litigation,” department spokeswoman Rebecca Ayers said in an e-mail. “The department followed appropriate procedures to put the regulation in place and the regulation is fully supported by law.”

The department promulgated the rule last month.

“Doctors and other health care providers should not be forced to choose between good professional standing and violating their conscience,” Health and Human Services Secretary Mike Leavitt said in a statement at the time. “This rule protects the right of medical providers to care for their patients in accord with their conscience.”

The department has said it believes that both the public and health care providers are unaware of the federal anti-discrimination laws.

“Many health care providers routinely face pressure to change their medical practice — often in direct opposition to their personal convictions,” the department’s assistant secretary of health, Adm. Joxel Garcia, said in a December statement. “During my practice as an OB-GYN, I witnessed this firsthand. Health care providers shouldn’t have to check their consciences at the hospital door. Fortunately, Congress enacted several laws to that end, but too many are unaware these protections exist.”

(CNN) — Seven states and two advocacy groups have taken legal action against the Bush administration, seeking to stop a federal rule that expands protections for health professionals who object on religious or ethical grounds to performing abortions or other procedures.

Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal filed one of the lawsuits Thursday for Connecticut, California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Oregon and Rhode Island. He argued that the rule threatens women’s access to health care and weakens state laws governing contraception.

Blumenthal described the regulation as a last-minute legal threat left by the outgoing Bush administration, scheduled to take effect on Inauguration Day. He said it could unlawfully and unnecessarily jeopardize women’s health and damage important constitutional protections.

According to Blumenthal, the rule deliberately creates additional, unwarranted uncertainty about what qualifies as abortion. He said that ambiguity could encourage health workers to adopt their own definitions and refuse nearly every type of birth control, including emergency contraception for rape survivors.

Separate lawsuits were also filed Thursday by the Planned Parenthood Federation of America and the American Civil Liberties Union. The ACLU brought its case on behalf of the National Family Planning & Reproductive Health Association.

The Department of Health and Human Services said the regulation permits the federal government to deny funding to state or local authorities, health insurance plans and medical facilities that fail to comply with existing federal statutes. Those laws prohibit discrimination against physicians and other health care employees who decline to take part in procedures such as abortions or sterilizations, or who refuse to refer patients for them.

Department spokeswoman Rebecca Ayers said by e-mail that officials had not yet reviewed the legal complaints and would address any pending cases in court. She added that HHS used the proper process to establish the rule and maintained that it has full legal support.

The department issued the regulation the previous month. At the time, Health and Human Services Secretary Mike Leavitt said doctors and other medical professionals should not have to decide between preserving their professional status and acting against their consciences. He said the rule safeguards providers’ ability to treat patients consistently with their moral convictions.

HHS has also said that many members of the public and the medical profession do not know about existing federal protections against such discrimination.

In a December statement, Assistant Secretary for Health Adm. Joxel Garcia said health care workers are frequently pressured to alter how they practice medicine, sometimes in direct conflict with their personal beliefs. Garcia said he had observed such situations himself while working as an obstetrician-gynecologist. He argued that medical professionals should not be required to abandon their consciences when entering a hospital and noted that Congress had passed several laws to protect them, although too few people were aware of those safeguards.

The rule, issued by the Department of Health and Human Services during the final weeks of President George W. Bush’s administration, applies to a broad range of federally funded health-care institutions and workers. It bars organizations receiving federal money from discriminating against employees who decline to perform, assist with, or in some circumstances refer patients for procedures they find objectionable. Institutions that fail to comply could lose federal funding.

The administration said the regulation was necessary to enforce existing federal “conscience” laws, including statutes protecting medical professionals who object to abortion or sterilization. Federal officials argued that some doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and other workers were unaware of those protections or feared professional retaliation for invoking them.

Opponents contend that the rule is written so broadly that it could interfere with patients’ access to lawful medical care. They say it may allow workers to withhold information, counseling, referrals, or services involving contraception, emergency contraception, infertility treatment, and other forms of reproductive care. The plaintiffs also argue that the regulation could conflict with state laws requiring hospitals and pharmacies to provide certain services or information.

The states maintain that the rule places federal funding at risk while leaving them uncertain about how to reconcile federal requirements with their own public-health and patient-protection laws. They warn that patients—particularly low-income women, people in rural communities, and those requiring urgent care—could face delays or be unable to obtain services if providers refuse to assist them without ensuring access elsewhere.

Planned Parenthood and the ACLU similarly argue that the regulation puts providers’ objections ahead of patients’ health and informed decision-making. They are asking the courts to prevent the rule from taking effect or to declare it invalid, asserting that HHS exceeded its authority and did not adequately consider its effect on access to care.

The federal government, however, says the regulation does not ban any medical procedure or require patients to share a provider’s beliefs. Instead, officials describe it as an enforcement mechanism designed to ensure that recipients of federal health funds respect long-standing legal protections against discrimination based on a worker’s refusal to participate in certain procedures.

The dispute therefore centers on how to balance two competing concerns: preserving patients’ access to comprehensive health care and protecting medical professionals from being forced to act against their religious convictions or moral beliefs.

# Seven states, Planned Parenthood and ACLU sue Bush administration over health worker rule

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Seven states, Planned Parenthood and the American Civil Liberties Union filed lawsuits Tuesday challenging a Bush administration rule designed to protect health care workers who refuse to participate in abortions or other medical procedures because of religious or moral objections.

The regulation, issued by the Department of Health and Human Services in the final weeks of President George W. Bush’s administration, allows the federal government to withhold funding from health care institutions that discriminate against employees who decline to provide certain services.

Connecticut, California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Oregon and Rhode Island filed one of the lawsuits in federal court in Connecticut. Planned Parenthood and the ACLU filed separate challenges.

The states argue that the rule is overly broad, conflicts with existing laws and could interfere with their ability to ensure patients receive complete medical information and timely care. Opponents also say its language could allow workers to refuse to provide contraception, counseling, referrals or other reproductive health services.

“The rule sacrifices patients’ rights and access to health care in favor of an individual provider’s personal beliefs,” the ACLU said in announcing its lawsuit.

Planned Parenthood said the regulation could threaten federal funding for hospitals and clinics that require employees to meet established standards of patient care.

Supporters of the rule argue that doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other health professionals should not be forced to take part in procedures they consider morally objectionable.

The Department of Health and Human Services has said the regulation is intended to enforce several existing federal “conscience” laws, some of which date to the 1970s. Those statutes generally prohibit recipients of federal funds from discriminating against health care workers who refuse to perform or assist with abortions and certain other procedures.

The rule applies to a wide range of health care employees and institutions receiving federal money. Critics contend that key terms are not clearly defined, potentially allowing protections to extend beyond those directly involved in a medical procedure.

The lawsuits ask federal judges to block the regulation and declare that HHS exceeded its authority in adopting it.

The rule was scheduled to take effect as President-elect Barack Obama prepared to take office. Obama had criticized the policy during the campaign, and his incoming administration was expected to review it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal’s multistate lawsuit challenging the Bush administration’s new “conscience” regulation for medical providers, including arguments from both the states and the Department of Health and Human Services.
counterfactuals.output:
## Overview

In January 2009, Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal led a coalition of seven states—Connecticut, California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Oregon, and Rhode Island—in federal court against the Department of Health and Human Services. The suit challenged a regulation issued during the closing weeks of President George W. Bush’s administration concerning health-care workers and institutions that object to participating in certain medical services on religious or moral grounds.

The final rule, published December 19, 2008, took effect January 20, 2009. It was formally titled **“Ensuring That Department of Health and Human Services Funds Do Not Support Coercive or Discriminatory Policies or Practices in Violation of Federal Law,”** codified at 45 C.F.R. Part 88.

## What the regulation did

The rule was intended to enforce three existing federal conscience-protection provisions:

- the **Church Amendments**, which protect certain individuals and institutions objecting to abortion or sterilization;
- Section 245 of the **Public Health Service Act**, covering discrimination involving abortion training and related activities; and
- the annual **Weldon Amendment**, barring certain federal funds from governments or agencies that discriminate against health-care entities because they do not provide, pay for, cover, or refer for abortions.

Recipients of HHS funds were required to certify compliance. HHS’s Office for Civil Rights was given enforcement responsibility, and noncompliance could potentially result in suspension, termination, or recovery of federal funds.

Although the final version omitted an especially controversial proposed definition of “abortion,” it retained broad language concerning who qualifies as a protected health-care entity and what it means to “assist in the performance” of a medical procedure.

## The states’ arguments

Blumenthal characterized the rule as a last-minute effort to place ideology over patients’ access to care. The states’ principal claims included:

1. **HHS exceeded its statutory authority.**  
   The states argued that the underlying federal conscience laws were limited in scope, while HHS had created a much broader right to refuse participation in medical care. In their view, an executive agency could enforce existing statutes but could not expand them by regulation.

2. **The rule was vague and overbroad.**  
   Terms such as “assist in the performance” could encompass not only doctors and nurses directly involved in a procedure, but pharmacists, counselors, laboratory personnel, receptionists, ambulance workers, schedulers, or others with an indirect connection to care.

3. **It threatened access to services beyond abortion.**  
   The coalition warned that the regulation could be invoked to refuse contraception, emergency contraception, sterilization, infertility treatment, counseling, referrals, or information about lawful medical options.

4. **It conflicted with state law and state health programs.**  
   States often require hospitals, pharmacies, and licensed professionals to provide emergency treatment, informed-consent information, referrals, or timely access to medication. The complaint argued that the federal rule disrupted those requirements and could prevent states from enforcing professional standards.

5. **It jeopardized federal funding.**  
   Because the certification requirement applied broadly to entities receiving HHS money, the states said disputes involving individual employees could place large amounts of Medicaid, public-health, research, and other federal assistance at risk. They contended that this was an impermissibly coercive and ambiguous condition on federal funds.

6. **HHS had not adequately justified the regulation.**  
   Under the Administrative Procedure Act, the states alleged that the agency acted arbitrarily and capriciously, failed to establish a genuine enforcement problem, and did not sufficiently address conflicts with emergency-care laws, Title VII employment protections, patients’ rights, and state regulation of medicine.

The states stressed that they were not seeking to eliminate legitimate statutory protections for religious objections. Their position was that the Bush administration had transformed narrowly drawn protections against discrimination into a sweeping refusal right without authorization from Congress.

## HHS’s defense

HHS presented the regulation as an enforcement measure, not as the creation of a new substantive right.

The department argued that:

- Congress had already enacted the conscience protections, and HHS was obligated to ensure that recipients of federal money obeyed them.
- Complaints and surveys indicated that some health-care professionals were being pressured to participate in, train for, refer for, or otherwise facilitate procedures to which they objected.
- Existing enforcement had been fragmented and poorly understood; assigning responsibility to the Office for Civil Rights and requiring certifications would make compliance more effective.
- The broad wording was necessary because coercion can occur through indirect assistance, not only through personally performing a procedure.
- The regulation did not automatically authorize any employee to refuse any task. Whether protection applied would depend on the relevant federal statute and the facts of the particular case.
- States and institutions accepting federal funds were already subject to federal conditions, and conflicting state requirements could not override federal conscience statutes.
- Loss of funding was not automatic; HHS retained discretion to seek voluntary compliance and use ordinary enforcement procedures.

HHS also maintained that protecting providers from discrimination could help preserve diversity in the medical workforce and allow religiously affiliated institutions and professionals to remain in health care.

## Subsequent developments

The case was filed as **Connecticut v. United States**, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Connecticut. Other organizations and states brought related challenges.

After President Barack Obama took office, HHS reconsidered the rule. In 2011, the department rescinded most of the Bush-era regulation, including its broad definitions and certification provisions, while leaving the underlying federal conscience statutes in force and preserving an enforcement role for HHS’s Office for Civil Rights. The rollback largely mooted the states’ challenge.

The central dispute therefore was not whether Congress had enacted some conscience protections—it plainly had—but whether the Bush administration had lawfully interpreted and enforced them or had instead created a much broader right to refuse involvement in patient care.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# States, cities and health groups challenge federal “conscience” rule over abortion and sterilization care

**WASHINGTON —** A sweeping federal regulation that could cut off government funding to hospitals, clinics and other health organizations accused of discriminating against workers who object to participating in abortions, sterilizations or related referrals is facing multiple legal challenges from states, local governments and reproductive-health providers.

The lawsuits contend that the Department of Health and Human Services exceeded its authority by creating an expansive enforcement system for existing federal conscience laws. Plaintiffs also argue that the regulation is unconstitutionally coercive because it threatens potentially broad losses of federal health funding and could interfere with emergency care, informed-consent rules and patients’ access to lawful services.

HHS has defended the rule as necessary to ensure that doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other health workers do not have to abandon their religious beliefs or moral convictions to keep their jobs.

At the center of the dispute is the department’s rule titled **“Protecting Statutory Conscience Rights in Health Care.”** Issued during the Trump administration, it directs HHS’s Office for Civil Rights to enforce more than two dozen federal statutes protecting individuals and organizations that object to providing, assisting with or referring for certain medical procedures.

Those laws include the Church Amendments, the Coats-Snowe Amendment and the Weldon Amendment, which contain protections related primarily to abortion and sterilization. The regulation also addresses objections involving assisted suicide, advance directives and some other forms of care.

## A broader definition of participation

The rule does not create the underlying conscience protections. Congress enacted those provisions over several decades. The legal fight instead concerns how far HHS may go in interpreting and enforcing them.

Among the regulation’s most disputed provisions are broad definitions of terms such as “assist in the performance,” “referral” and “discrimination.” Critics say those definitions could allow a wide range of workers—not only clinicians directly involved in a procedure—to refuse tasks that they believe facilitate objectionable care.

Depending on the circumstances, that could include scheduling an appointment, providing information, arranging transportation, processing paperwork or directing a patient to another provider, the challengers argue.

The rule also requires recipients of federal health funds to provide written assurances and certifications of compliance. HHS may investigate complaints and, if it finds a violation, pursue remedies that can include suspending or terminating federal assistance or referring the matter to the Justice Department.

State and local officials say the threatened financial consequences are far out of proportion to any authority Congress gave HHS. Because hospitals and public-health systems often receive money through numerous federal programs, they argue, the regulation could put billions of dollars at risk over a dispute involving a single employee.

HHS has said enforcement would be based on the applicable statute and funding stream and would follow established procedures. The department argues that meaningful remedies are essential because conscience protections have little value if institutions can ignore them without consequence.

## States and cities allege federal overreach

New York and a coalition of other states and local governments filed one of the principal challenges in federal court in Manhattan. Related cases were brought by California, San Francisco, Washington, Oregon and other jurisdictions, as well as by organizations including Planned Parenthood and the National Family Planning & Reproductive Health Association.

The government plaintiffs say they already have laws and workplace policies that seek to balance employees’ religious rights with patients’ rights and institutions’ obligations to provide care. The federal regulation, they argue, disrupts that balance by elevating an objecting worker’s preferences over other legal duties.

Their complaints raise several major claims:

- **Administrative Procedure Act:** The challengers say HHS adopted an arbitrary and capricious rule, failed to justify its expansion of existing law and did not adequately consider the effects on patients and health systems.
- **Lack of statutory authority:** Congress, they argue, enacted specific conscience protections but did not authorize HHS to rewrite them through broad regulatory definitions or create a new, department-wide enforcement regime.
- **Spending Clause concerns:** States say the federal government may not attach vague, unexpected or coercive conditions to funding, particularly when the threatened loss could extend beyond money directly connected to an alleged violation.
- **Separation of powers:** The lawsuits contend that HHS effectively amended acts of Congress by expanding their reach and remedies.
- **Conflict with other laws:** Plaintiffs argue that the rule may clash with federal and state requirements governing emergency treatment, patient information, nondiscrimination, professional licensing and employee accommodations.
- **Constitutional claims:** Some challengers maintain that the rule favors religious objections in a way that may violate the Establishment Clause, while also depriving states of clear notice about the conditions attached to federal funds.

The challengers emphasize that the cases are not an attempt to eliminate all conscience rights. Instead, they say the issue is whether HHS may impose a uniform and unusually broad interpretation of those rights while threatening the funding needed to operate public hospitals, Medicaid programs and other services.

## Concerns about emergencies and patient access

Health organizations challenging the rule warn that its effects could be especially serious in rural areas or other communities where patients have few alternatives.

A refusal to provide an abortion referral, for example, may leave a patient unable to find a provider within the period when the procedure is legal or medically available. Critics also say refusals to discuss sterilization can affect patients making time-sensitive decisions during childbirth or other medical treatment.

Another concern involves emergencies. Federal law generally requires hospital emergency departments to screen and stabilize patients with urgent medical conditions. States and medical groups argue that the conscience rule does not clearly explain how institutions should respond if an employee’s refusal conflicts with a patient’s immediate medical needs.

Providers also say the regulation could complicate compliance with informed-consent requirements. A health organization may be obligated to tell patients about their diagnosis and available treatment options even when an individual employee objects to discussing or facilitating one of those options.

The rule’s opponents further argue that health systems could struggle to guarantee services if workers may decline peripheral duties without advance notice. Although employers often accommodate religious objections through scheduling or reassignment, plaintiffs say the federal regulation could make it harder to determine when an accommodation is reasonable and when it imposes an undue burden on patients or other employees.

## HHS says existing protections were neglected

HHS and supporters of the regulation describe the lawsuits as an attack on long-standing federal law.

They point to complaints from health professionals who say they were pressured to participate in procedures they considered morally objectionable, denied employment or training opportunities, or punished after raising conscience concerns. In the department’s view, previous enforcement was inconsistent and lacked clear procedures.

The agency says the regulation gives workers and funding recipients notice of their rights and responsibilities. It also argues that organizations accepting federal money must comply with the conditions Congress placed on those funds.

Religious-liberty groups supporting the rule say conscience protections are necessary to maintain a diverse health-care workforce. Without strong safeguards, they argue, professionals who oppose abortion or sterilization could be forced out of medicine, nursing and related fields.

Supporters also reject the claim that the regulation authorizes blanket denials of care. They say its application depends on the text of the particular federal statute involved and that disputes can often be resolved through staffing adjustments or other accommodations.

## A dispute over the scale of enforcement

A central question for the courts is how much leverage HHS may use to enforce the conscience statutes.

The challengers argue that Congress sometimes tied a particular protection to a specific grant or program. HHS, they say, cannot transform those targeted conditions into a threat against every dollar a hospital, state agency or health system receives from the department.

The federal government counters that agencies traditionally have authority to enforce funding conditions and to take action when recipients violate federal law. It also disputes the characterization that every violation would automatically result in the loss of all HHS funding.

The cases therefore turn not only on abortion policy or religious liberty, but also on broader questions of administrative law: how agencies interpret statutes, what conditions the federal government may attach to grants and how clearly those conditions must be communicated.

The plaintiffs are asking the courts to declare the rule unlawful and block its enforcement. Because the suits involve overlapping claims and affect health systems nationwide, the litigation could determine how federal conscience protections are applied well beyond the specific organizations and governments that brought the cases.

### States, Medical Groups Oppose Bush Administration’s Provider Conscience Rule

**WASHINGTON —** A Bush administration regulation expanding federal protections for health care workers who decline to participate in services they find morally or religiously objectionable drew opposition from several states, reproductive-rights organizations and medical groups, which argued that the rule could restrict patients’ access to contraception and other lawful care.

The Department of Health and Human Services issued the final rule in December 2008. It required recipients of certain federal funds to certify compliance with existing laws protecting health care providers who object to participating in abortions or other procedures on religious or moral grounds.

HHS Secretary Mike Leavitt defended the regulation as necessary to ensure that medical professionals are not penalized for their beliefs.

“Doctors and other health care providers should not be forced to choose between good professional standing and violating their conscience,” Leavitt said in announcing the rule.

Assistant Secretary for Health Adm. Joxel Garcia similarly argued that entering the medical profession should not require workers to relinquish their moral convictions. “The freedom of conscience is not to be surrendered upon issuance of a medical degree,” Garcia said.

Opponents said the regulation’s definitions were broad enough to reach beyond abortion and could allow workers to refuse involvement in contraception, sterilization, infertility treatment or other services. They also argued that the rule did not adequately balance providers’ objections against patients’ rights to timely medical information and treatment.

Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal, who joined other state officials in challenging the regulation, described it as “a breathtakingly broad and vague rule” that could endanger access to reproductive health services.

Medical organizations also raised concerns that the regulation could conflict with professional obligations requiring clinicians to inform patients of available treatments or refer them to another provider. Supporters countered that referral or counseling can itself amount to participation in conduct a worker considers objectionable.

The dispute centered partly on the rule’s scope. Federal statutes already prohibited discrimination against certain health care entities and professionals who declined to perform or assist with abortions. The Bush administration maintained that stronger enforcement was needed because some workers were unaware of those protections or feared professional retaliation. Critics said the new regulation expanded those laws without sufficiently defining which services or employees were covered.

Several states and advocacy groups sought to block or overturn the rule, contending that it could interfere with state laws governing emergency care, informed consent and access to contraception. The controversy left the incoming Obama administration to decide whether to retain, revise or rescind the regulation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the controversy over the HHS regulation protecting doctors and other health workers who object to certain medical procedures, noting concerns about contraception access and the administration’s defense of the rule.
counterfactuals.output:
The HHS “conscience” rule strengthened protections for doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and other health workers who refuse to participate in procedures they oppose on religious or moral grounds, particularly abortion and sterilization.

Opponents argued that its broad language could also allow workers or institutions to deny, withhold information about, or refuse referrals for birth control—including emergency contraception—potentially limiting access for women, especially in rural or underserved areas. They also warned that patients’ needs were being subordinated to providers’ beliefs.

The administration defended the rule as an enforcement and clarification of existing federal conscience laws, not a new restriction on contraception. Officials said it was intended to prevent health workers from being forced to violate deeply held beliefs and maintained that it neither defined contraception as abortion nor authorized providers to obstruct patients from obtaining lawful care elsewhere.
